title: Who's afraid of the big band bond vigilantes?
gist: A weekly UK policy digest argues that this week's spike in gilt yields (5.2%, highest since 2007) is being overplayed as a market-panic story when it actually reflects historically normal borrowing costs versus an unusual 2010s/early-2020s low-rate anomaly, while also flagging AI's homogenizing effect on writing style, the UK's uniquely bad post-2008 productivity slump, and a sharp rise in teen loneliness and falling life satisfaction among UK youth.

themes.theme: Gilt yields: normal levels, not a crisis

insights.claim: UK government borrowing costs (gilt yields) reached 5.2% this week, the highest since 2007, but when viewed against a chart of UK borrowing costs since 1751 (when Henry Pelham first consolidated government debt into one bond), current rates are actually close to the historical average — it is the ultra-low borrowing costs of the 2010s and early 2020s that were the true anomaly.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A contrarian framing that should temper panic-driven gilt-market narratives: investors should treat 5%+ yields as a reversion to historical norms rather than a crisis signal, reducing the case for assuming an imminent UK debt crisis purely from yield-level headlines.

insights.claim: Daily media focus on gilt-yield moves is 'yet again unwarranted' — Tuesday's widely reported move was only about 0.07 percentage points, which is not unusual, and the broader rise this week arguably reflects concerns that central banks will raise rates to counter rising oil prices rather than anything the UK Prime Minister said.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Reattributes the proximate driver of gilt moves from domestic political noise to global oil-price-driven central bank rate expectations — relevant for separating genuine UK fiscal-credibility risk from broader global rate-repricing when trading UK rates/FX.

insights.claim: The UK is now paying over £130 billion a year in debt interest, more than £100 billion higher than during the pandemic, and the piece argues Chancellor Rachel Reeves ('Mr Healey' in the original, likely referring to the Chancellor) should not bank on ultra-low rates returning, implying taxes and spending need to adjust to a structurally higher-rate world.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A concrete, large fiscal number (£130bn annual debt interest, +£100bn vs pandemic levels) framing the scale of the UK's structural fiscal challenge — directly relevant to forecasting UK tax/spending policy and gilt supply going forward.
insights.locator: Chart of the week section, closing lines

insights.claim: A study analyzing over 800,000 texts found that AI editing reduced the variation in writing complexity by up to half; even though the core meaning of AI-'polished' human texts was preserved, it became significantly harder to infer the original authors' personal characteristics because distinctive linguistic cues were watered down.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Quantifies a specific, measurable homogenization effect of AI writing tools — relevant to any business relying on writing-style analysis (fraud detection, authorship verification, personalized marketing) as AI editing becomes ubiquitous and erodes those signals.
insights.quote: AI editing reduced the variation in writing complexity by up to half.

insights.claim: UK market-sector productivity has grown just 0.5% a year since 2008, well behind the US (1.7%) and eurozone (1.0%), and down sharply from 2.5% annual growth in the previous two decades; a Bank Underground analysis attributes the UK's especially large slowdown partly to faster manufacturing shrinkage and partly to Brexit, expected to have knocked off an additional 3.25% by 2028.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Provides a quantified, internationally-benchmarked productivity gap and an explicit Brexit growth-cost estimate (3.25% by 2028) — a concrete data point for modeling UK long-run GDP potential and equity risk premium versus US/eurozone peers.

insights.claim: Recent UK productivity data diverges sharply by measurement method: the ONS Labour Force Survey shows productivity falling 0.2% in the year to Q2 2026, while HMRC's more accurate administrative data shows productivity growing 1.1%, better than even the late-2010s' 0.7% pace — suggesting the 'productivity gloom' narrative may be a measurement artifact.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A meaningful data-quality caveat: analysts citing UK productivity stagnation should specify data source, since the 'more accurate' HMRC admin data tells a materially more optimistic story — relevant for reassessing bearish UK growth theses built on survey-based productivity stats.

themes.theme: Green industrial policy: jobs impact is limited, political impact is contested

insights.claim: New research on the US Inflation Reduction Act found that IRA-designated areas (fossil-fuel-dependent, high-unemployment) saw a 144% rise in the probability of landing a solar project, but the associated jobs had little employment effect and the projects did not shift local political sentiment — contradicting an earlier paper the Foundation had cited showing a rise in Democratic presidential vote share from IRA-linked plants.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Casts doubt on the political-payoff thesis for green industrial policy in swing/fossil-fuel-dependent regions, suggesting the electoral case for clean-energy siting strategy may be weaker or more visibility-dependent than assumed — relevant for assessing durability of US climate/industrial policy support.

insights.claim: A six-month Resolution Foundation deep dive into Aberdeen and Grimsby found significant net-zero economic potential in both, but concluded the UK Government needs a more deliberate, hands-on approach to concentrate green industries — to cushion oil's decline in Aberdeen and to form a new local-economy anchor in Grimsby — beyond simply drilling at the Jackdaw gas field.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Identifies two specific UK regional economies (Aberdeen, Grimsby) where targeted green-industrial policy intervention is recommended — relevant for regional UK investment and infrastructure policy tracking.

themes.theme: Masculinity, labor market outcomes, and mental health

insights.claim: A survey of over 100,000 men across 70 countries found stereotypically 'manly' traits (competitiveness, violence, reluctance to ask for help) are surprisingly stable across countries, and men scoring higher on these metrics are five percentage points more likely to be employed, earn nearly 3% more, and work in stereotypically male industries — but are also more likely to take risks, report higher depression, and less likely to seek mental-health help.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Quantifies a real labor-market wage/employment premium tied to masculine-coded traits alongside a documented mental-health cost — relevant to workplace-culture, DEI, and mental-health-benefit policy design for employers.

insights.claim: The same study found that exposure to war or economic recession during one's formative years increases self-reported feelings of masculinity, implying that macro shocks (conflict, recessions) causally shape gendered behavioral norms that later show up in labor-market and health outcomes.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Suggests current macro shocks (e.g., the ongoing Iran-related conflict, cost-of-living pressures) could be shaping a new generational cohort's behavioral and labor-market norms for decades — a long-horizon social/demographic variable for workforce planning.

themes.theme: UK youth loneliness and declining life satisfaction

insights.claim: The share of UK 16-21-year-olds reporting no close friends rose from 1 in 100 a decade ago to 1 in 20 today, while life satisfaction among young men has dropped from over half to just under two-fifths since the 2010s, and the share of young people reporting they accomplish less due to mental health has quadrupled over the same period.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: A stark, quantified deterioration in UK youth social and mental wellbeing over one decade — relevant to long-run labor-force productivity, healthcare demand, and consumer-sector (social/leisure) planning around a generation with weakened social capital.

insights.claim: The Foundation attributes declining friendship quantity/quality among UK youth partly to falling self-confidence — only a third of young women report being happy with how they look — and links this to their own prior research showing young people are now alone up to two hours more per day than a decade ago, partly due to lone/isolated working arrangements.
insights.speaker: Resolution Foundation
insights.so_what: Connects declining youth social confidence to structural labor-market changes (lone working, e.g., remote/gig work), suggesting the shift toward isolated work arrangements has a measurable social cost for the youngest workforce cohort.
insights.locator: Kids these days section, closing lines
